nucleus_explanation: Radius ≈ {r} fm: the atom is ~{ratio} times bigger.
Almost all the mass of the atom is here. Fly closer (or press Enter) to go in.
cloud_explanation: Each dot is a likely position of an electron, not a path: electrons do not orbit.
Colours: one per shell, n = 1 (orange) to n = 7. p, d and f orbitals show their lobes. O: one subshell at a time.
Electrons are elementary particles: there is nothing inside them.
cloud_explanation_realistic: Isolated atom in its ground state: averaged over all orientations, its density is spherical.
Electrons are elementary particles: there is nothing inside them.
atom.time: Stationary orbitals: the density does not change (the twinkling = successive measurements)

shape.s: s orbital: a sphere (with {nodes} spherical nodes inside).
shape.p: p orbitals: two lobes (a figure of eight) along x, y or z.
shape.d: d orbitals: four-leaf clovers, and dz²: two lobes with a ring around the middle.
shape.f: f orbitals: six or eight lobes; the most complex shapes in the ground states.

atom.hund: Hund's rule: electrons first take empty orbitals (↑), then pair up (↑↓).
atom.full: Full subshell: its orbitals add up to a perfect sphere (Unsöld's theorem).
atom.partial: Partly filled: several states are equally good; this is one of them.
atom.realistic_subshell: Realistic mode: averaged over orientations, every subshell is spherical.
atom.orbital_colors: Each orbital in its own colour. I: one orbital at a time.
plastic: Plastic mode: each green ball (e⁻) is an electron. They orbit as in Bohr's model (1913).
In reality they have no size and no path: they are probability clouds (Tab: other modes).
In the centre, the nucleus with its protons (+) and neutrons (0), to scale: tiny.

nucleus.title: {protons} + {neutrons} · radius ≈ {r} fm
explanation: The strong force beats the electric repulsion between the {protons}.
Chance of finding an electron in here: ~{p_in}
A teaspoon of nuclear matter would weigh ~1,000 million tonnes.
explanation_hydrogen: The hydrogen-1 nucleus is a single proton.
Chance of finding the electron in here: ~{p_in}
explanation_realistic: Density of nuclear matter (Woods–Saxon profile): nucleons are quantum
waves and have no definite position.
nucleus.strong_lines: Green lines: strong nuclear force (range ~2 fm).
nucleus.go_in: fly closer (or press Enter) to go in

proton.title: Proton
proton.detail: charge +1 · {mass} MeV/c² · quarks u u d
explanation: 3 valence quarks (uud) held together by gluons.
Only ~1 % of its mass comes from the quarks: the rest is energy

neutron.title: Neutron
neutron.detail: charge 0 · {mass} MeV/c² · quarks u d d
explanation: 3 valence quarks (udd). A free neutron decays in ~15 minutes;
inside a stable nucleus it lasts forever.
Without neutrons, the electric repulsion would push the protons apart.

nucleus.time: 1 s on screen ≈ 10⁻²² s (a nucleon crosses the nucleus in ~10⁻²² s)
plastic: Plastic mode: protons (+, red) and neutrons (0, blue). The colours are made up.
They are not hard balls: each one is a cloud of quarks and gluons ~0.84 fm in radius.

nucleon.title: {name}: valence quarks {content} + parton sea
quark_explanation: Fundamental particle: no known structure (< 10⁻¹⁸ m).
End of the journey: there is nothing 'inside' a quark.
Confinement: if you pull a quark away, the gluon tube breaks
explanation: Red/green/blue = colour charge (a label, not a real colour).
The 3 quarks add up to 'white'. Travelling gluons swap the colour
between them. Background dots: gluons and sea pairs.
The quarks are ~1 % of the mass; the rest is energy (E = mc²).
explanation_realistic: Parton fog: quarks, antiquarks and gluons that appear and
disappear. You cannot point at each quark: only the probability
nucleon.time: 1 s on screen ≈ 10⁻²⁴ s (light crosses a proton in ~3×10⁻²⁴ s)
plastic: Plastic mode: up (u) and down (d) quarks; the gluon (g) travels from one to another.
The halo of each quark is its colour charge (red, green or blue): a label, not a colour.
Quarks are point-like: here they are balls so you can see them.
